tags: square enclosure, round barrow, cairn, roman, pre-roman
description:
This is an Early Medieval Royal Pictish site exhibiting evidence of religious activity spanning from at least the Iron Age. A square ditched enclosure on the periphery is of particular interest, as it incorporates a space used since the Bronze Age. Pits from this earlier period, packed with stones and charcoal, suggest either domestic or ceremonial use. Aside from a single residual Neolithic sample, no organic material was recovered from the ditch, which clearly overcuts Bronze Age features. The enclosure is tentatively dated to the 1st–4th century CE based on morphological comparisons to sites like Rhynie, Rutland, Hayling Island, and Gosbecks, as well as the assumed use of Roman construction techniques. These parallels suggest the structure served as a shrine or ceremonial site. Immediately to the east, a round barrow burial dating to 410–530 CE likely featured an above-ground structure.

A sherd of Scottish White Gritty ware (13th–14th century CE) found in a re-cut ditch provides a terminus ante quem for the site's primary use. Inside the enclosure, a pit containing a burnt ash box, wheat grain, and a knife blade was initially interpreted as ritualistic. However, once dated to 1310–1440 CE, this interpretation was dismissed without an alternative being proposed.

To the south, a central Bronze Age cairn reveals Iron Age/Roman activity dated to 20–140 CE. Evidence shows a period of burning within a pit cut into the cairn, which later silted up and was paved over. Further burnt material and animal bone found atop this paving suggest votive activity, echoing Roman-era practices observed at Tara, Newgrange, and Mine Howe.
bibliography: Campbell, Ewan, and Stephen T Driscoll. Royal Forteviot: Excavations at a Pictish Power Centre in Eastern Scotland. [object Object], 2020. https://doi.org/10.5284/1082003.
